In [[mathematics]], a '''locally finite measure''' is a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] for which every point of the [[measure space]] has a [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of [[Finite set|finite]] measure.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Berge|first=Claude|title=Topological Spaces|year=1963|isbn=0486696537|pages=31}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Gemignani|first=Michael C.|title=Elementary Topology|year=1972|isbn=0486665224|pages=228}}</ref>

==Definition==

Let <math>(X, T)</math> be a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[topological space]] and let <math>\Sigma</math> be a [[sigma algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>X</math> that contains the topology <math>T</math> (so that every [[open set]] is a [[measurable set]], and <math>\Sigma</math> is at least as fine as the [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>X</math>). A measure/[[signed measure]]/[[complex measure]] <math>\mu</math> defined on <math>\Sigma</math> is called '''locally finite''' if, for every point <math>p</math> of the space <math>X,</math> there is an open [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] <math>N_p</math> of <math>p</math> such that the <math>\mu</math>-measure of <math>N_p</math> is finite.

In more condensed notation, <math>\mu</math> is locally finite [[if and only if]]
<math display=block>\text{for all } p \in X, \text{ there exists } N_p \in T \mbox{ such that } p \in N_p \mbox{ and } \left|\mu\left(N_p\right)\right| < + \infty.</math>

==Examples==

# Any [[probability measure]] on <math>X</math> is locally finite, since it assigns unit measure to the whole space. Similarly, any measure that assigns finite measure to the whole space is locally finite.
# [[Lebesgue measure]] on [[Euclidean space]] is locally finite.
# By definition, any [[Radon measure]] is locally finite.
# The [[counting measure]] is sometimes locally finite and sometimes not: the counting measure on the [[integer]]s with their usual [[discrete topology]] is locally finite, but the counting measure on the [[real line]] with its usual Borel [[topology]] is not.
